GBUS 461 · Week 9 Lab · Spot the Leakage · StreamNow+

Spotting Leakage

Can you tell which features exist at scoring time — and which ones are secretly from the future?

The Timing Rule

A feature is valid only if it is available at the exact moment the model scores every customer. If it comes from after the scoring date — even by a single day — it is leakage. It makes the model look extraordinary in testing and worthless in production.

Feature Classification
FeatureStatusWhy
tenure_monthsSAFEKnown at scoring time for every subscriber
avg_watch_hours_30dSAFEPast 30-day window ending on scoring date
support_tickets_90dSAFEHistorical count, available on scoring date
payment_failures_90dSAFEHistorical billing data, known at scoring
cancel_page_views_next_7dLEAKAGEOccurs after scoring date — customer hasn't visited yet
refund_next_14dLEAKAGEFuture refund event — impossible to know on scoring date
The AUC Proof
0.517
Clean model AUC
Modest but honest
~0.91
With leakage AUC
Fake — model sees the future
Takeaway
  • The score jump from 0.517 to 0.91 is not intelligence — it is a lookup table disguised as a prediction model. Always ask: could I know this for every customer at exactly the moment I score them?
GBUS 461 · Week 9 · Mini-Case · Overfitting & Regularization

Which Model Ships?

Model A has better training numbers. Model B works better in the real world. Which one do you deploy?

The Case
Model A — Do Not Ship
  • Training accuracy: 74%
  • Validation accuracy: 60%
  • Gap: 14 percentage points
  • Classic overfitting — memorised the sample
Model B — Ship This
  • Training accuracy: 71%
  • Validation accuracy: 67%
  • Gap: 4 percentage points
  • Generalises to fresh data
Overfitting vs Regularization
  • Overfitting: training error keeps improving while validation error gets worse — the model memorises yesterday and fails tomorrow
  • Ridge regularization: shrinks all coefficients toward zero — useful when many correlated features carry overlapping signal (clicks, opens, watch hours)
  • Lasso: shrinks some coefficients to exactly zero — regularisation plus feature selection in one step
  • In StreamNow+: with 12+ behavioural signals, a Lasso model would likely drop 3–4 redundant predictors and improve generalisation
Takeaway
  • Ship Model B — a slightly simpler model that is stable on fresh data beats a flashy model that only wins on the training set
  • Before dismissing Model A entirely: apply regularization (Ridge or Lasso) and re-evaluate — the gap may close
GBUS 461 · Week 9 Lab · Decision Threshold · StreamNow+

Choosing the Threshold

0.50 is not sacred. The economics of the decision — not habit — should set the cutoff.

Break-Even Logic
  • Offer cost = $15 · Expected value if a true churner is saved = $120
  • Break-even threshold: p* = $15 ÷ $120 = 0.125
  • Any customer with a predicted churn probability ≥ 12.5% is worth targeting — the offer pays for itself in expected value
  • Setting the threshold at 0.50 (the arbitrary default) misses $1,568 in expected value vs the optimal
Four Options Compared
Option Threshold Targeted % of base Total EV
Too broad0.1029966%$1,904
Recommended ★0.12522851%$2,025
Close0.1518140%$1,963
Too conservative0.208721%$1,418
Arbitrary default0.50~164%~$457
Takeaway
  • Use p=0.125 — it is the economic break-even, not a guess; any score above it has positive expected value
  • Pre-commit the threshold before looking at results — setting it after you see the data is p-hacking by a different name

Building the Scorecard

From six raw event tables to one campaign-day scorecard — defined, joined, QA'd, and defended.

Business Question

"Which campaigns are actually generating value — and which are just buying traffic?"

Owner · Marketing Analytics / Campaign Operations

Role · Build an analysis-ready scorecard from raw event logs; engineer 8+ features; document QA evidence

Data
SourceGBUS 461 Week 3 Lab Data (synthetic)
WindowFeb 1 – Feb 14, 2026 · 14-day period
GrainOne campaign on one calendar day · 97 rows · keys: campaign_id + date
Tables joinedsessions → events → orders → campaign_spend → campaign_meta
Key variablessessions, clicks, add_to_cart, orders, revenue (from orders table — avoids order_items fanout), spend, channel, is_new_user
Method
  • Chose grain before writing any formula — campaign × day; keys campaign_id + date

  • Ran 5 required QA checks: key uniqueness, row count pre/post merge, missingness audit, sanity bounds, 3-row end-to-end spot check

Key Results & Interpretation
  • Email (C05) converts at 7.9% and ROAS 0.13× — best on both dimensions despite the smallest session count
  • Organic (C06) drives 22.7% of sessions but only 3.6% of revenue — high volume, low intent
  • 0 duplicate keys across 97 rows; 2.5% missing user_id; 4.6% missing campaign_id (dark/direct traffic)
  • ROAS_7d flagged as least-trusted metric — rolling revenue numerator against daily spend denominator; windows mismatched by design
  • Leakage note: revenue intentionally sourced from orders table, not order_items, to prevent fanout inflation
Recommendation
  • Do not scale Email budget on this scorecard alone — Email surfaces to high-intent, brand-aware users; the CVR advantage is structural, not necessarily causal
  • 4.6% missing campaign_id is a tracking gap that needs ops investigation before any budget decision
  • Run a holdout experiment to test Email's true incremental lift → that is exactly what Project 2 addresses

Running the A/B Test

Does a personalised Starbucks push notification drive incremental purchases — and does it hold up on margin?

Business Question

"Should we roll the personalized push offer out to all Rewards users — and what would we be giving up on margin if we did?"

Owner · CRM / Loyalty Marketing

Role · Design, run, and interpret an A/B experiment; check MDE; evaluate guardrail metrics; decide: scale / pause / run longer / redesign

Data
Sourcestarbucks_ab_synthetic.csv — generated by Starbucks_synthetic_AB_demowk6.r (seed=461)
Window14-day observation window · one scoring period
GrainOne Rewards member per row · Control: 19,927 · Treat: 20,073
Tables joinedSingle flat file — arm assigned at randomisation
Key variablesarm · exposed (compliance 92%) · converted · revenue · margin (−3pp for exposed) · unsub (guardrail) · segment (low/mid/high)
Method
  • Intent-to-treat (ITT): compared treat vs control on all assigned users regardless of push-open; preserves randomisation
  • Two-proportion z-test for conversion and unsub; t-test for margin per user
  • MDE computed at α=0.05, power=0.80 and compared against actual observed lift
  • Wald estimator for treatment-on-treated (TOT): ITT margin ÷ compliance delta (0.9202)
  • Segment breakdown (low / mid / high) to test effect heterogeneity

Key Results & Interpretation
  • Conversion lift of +0.42pp is significant (p=0.024) but below the MDE of 0.50pp — this test was underpowered to reliably detect that effect size
  • Margin lift of +$0.014 is not significant (p=0.51; CI: −$0.028 to +$0.055) — could easily be noise
  • High segment is the alarm: margin drops $0.108 despite slightly better conversion — the discount cannibalises the most profitable users
  • Unsub rate +0.12pp is directionally bad but not yet significant (p=0.28); at scale this matters
  • TOT (Wald): $0.015 margin lift per actually-exposed user — still not significant
Recommendation
  • Do not scale — the conversion signal exists but margin evidence is insufficient
  • Redesign: exclude high-engagement users from the discount tier, or reduce offer value for the High segment specifically
  • Run longer: extend to n=80k per arm to power the 0.50pp MDE properly
  • Pre-commit hard stop before next run: if unsub rate exceeds 1.5%, pause immediately

Predicting Who Churns

Logistic regression on clean features — no leakage — to decide who gets the $15 retention credit.

Business Question

"Which StreamNow+ subscribers are most likely to cancel in the next 30 days — and at what probability threshold does offering a $15 credit make economic sense?"

Owner · CRM / Subscriber Retention

Role · Build a clean logistic regression churn model; identify and remove leakage; select decision threshold from economics

Data
SourceGBUS461_Week9_StreamNow_Data.xlsx (synthetic, one scoring month)
WindowMarch 2026 · one-month prediction horizon
GrainOne subscriber per row · n=1,500 · churn rate 15.1% (227/1,500)
Tables joinedSingle flat file — no joins required
Key variablestenure_months · autopay · discount_flag · devices_linked · email_opens_30d · avg_watch_hours_30d · recent_login_gap_days · support_tickets_90d · payment_failures_90d · competitor_index · EXCLUDED: cancel_page_views_next_7d · refund_next_14d (leakage — occur after scoring date)
Method
  • Leakage audit first — cancel_page_views_next_7d and refund_next_14d removed; both only exist after scoring date
  • 70 / 30 train-test split · logistic regression · standard-scaled predictors
  • Model evaluated on holdout: AUC, calibration by quintile
  • Break-even threshold derived from economics: p* = $15 ÷ $120 = 0.125
  • Four thresholds compared by total expected value; feature importance ranked by |coefficient|

Key Results & Interpretation
  • Clean AUC = 0.517 — modest, honest; no leakage inflating the number
  • With leakage (cancel_page_views_next_7d) included, AUC jumps to ~0.91 — fake improvement; model is peeking at who has already started cancelling
  • 0–6 month cohort churns at 19.6% — highest risk, clearest intervention window
  • Autopay is the single strongest clean predictor — no autopay = no friction to cancel
  • Threshold p=0.125 maximises expected value at $2,025 across 228 targeted users (51% of test set)
Recommendation
  • Send the $15 credit to all subscribers scoring ≥ 0.125 — this is the economic break-even; going higher leaves value behind
  • Prioritise the 0–6 month cohort with proactive outreach — 19.6% churn rate, highest ROI on the intervention
  • Run a holdout (withhold credit from a random 20%) to confirm the model actually reduces churn vs organic retention
  • Retrain monthly — never deploy a March model into May without refitting on fresh scoring data

Pricing Under Inflation

When 68% of consumers switch brands on price, does your pricing playbook still hold?

Business Question

"How should brands reprice during sustained inflation — and why do MMMs built on pre-2021 data get this systematically wrong?"

Owner · Brand / Revenue Management

Role · Present a current-issues briefing on price elasticity under inflation; build and demo a live AI pricing tool

Data & Method
  • Secondary research: Nielsen consumer switching data 2019–2023 · SignalFire 2025 State of Tech Talent report · peer-reviewed MMM literature
  • Built PriceIQ™ live on the Anthropic Claude API — takes a plain-language pricing scenario, returns elasticity estimate, risk rating, and recommendation in seconds
  • Scenario modelling: ran three repricing strategies against a 12% price increase target and compared volume impact
  • Paired verbal presentation delivered to class; written brief submitted
Key Visual — Volume Impact by Pricing Strategy
Strategy
Price Δ

Hold price flat

Key Results & Interpretation
  • 68% of consumers switched brands on price in 2022–23 — up from 41% pre-pandemic; standard MMMs missed the structural break
  • Staggered repricing (6%+6% over 90 days) cuts volume loss by nearly half vs single-step: −10.4% vs −18.6%
  • MMMs trained on pre-2021 data systematically underestimate current price elasticity — they were calibrated in a low-inflation regime
  • PriceIQ™ demonstrated live in class: a brand manager with no data science background can run a pricing scenario check in under 30 seconds
Recommendation
  • Stagger any price increase over at least two steps separated by 45–90 days — the volume data is clear
  • Rebuild MMMs with post-2022 data before any budget allocation decision in an inflationary environment
  • Use PriceIQ™ or equivalent tools for rapid pre-decision scenario testing across pricing options

Consumer Analytical Insights

Understanding why people choose what they choose.

Consumer Price Sensitivity Segmentation — Inflation Era (GBUS 461)

Context: During 2022–23, 68% of consumers switched brands based on price — up from 41% pre-pandemic. Standard demographic segmentation missed these behavioural shifts entirely.

Analysis identified four behavioural segments that better predict purchasing behaviour under inflation: Value Seekers (34%), Trade-Down Risk (28%), Price Loyalists (19%), and Brand Agnostic (19%).

Strategic implication: Value Seekers respond to smart promotional architecture — not blanket discounts. Targeting them analytically retains more revenue than broad price cuts.

whisper Consumer Target Profile — ROAR Organics Brand Extension

Target: Wellness-oriented women, 22–43. Primary occasion: evening wind-down and relaxation — entirely unserved by ROAR's existing daytime hydration equity.

Perceptual mapping confirmed zero cannibalisation — whisper occupies a distinct quadrant on the legitimacy vs. relaxation axis away from all existing ROAR SKUs and from competitors (Recess, Moment, Trip, Refrezz).

Key insight: Only 12% of the $432B wellness market is served by functional hydration for relaxation occasions — a massive white space.

Whisper — Lavender Chamomile, Honey Lemon, Blueberry Vanilla

AI in Data Analytics

Marketing and consumer behaviour, taken apart and examined.

AI & Workforce Restructuring Across Career Stages — GBUS 461 Research

Research Question: How does AI affect productivity and career structure differently at entry-level, mid-level, senior, and managerial roles — in tech versus non-tech industries?

Brynjolfsson, Li & Raymond (2025) show AI delivers a 15% average productivity boost to novice workers — the largest gains at the bottom of the career ladder — while simultaneously compressing the learning curve that historically built judgment in senior roles.

SignalFire's 2025 State of Tech Talent report: new-graduate hiring in big tech down over 50% from 2019 levels, even as output per engineer rises.

Implication: Competitive advantage belongs to firms that calibrate AI augmentation by career stage — not those that simply automate fastest.

Predictive Modelling Deep-Dive — Key Determinants of Cardiovascular Disease (BIS 456)

Dataset: 918 patient records from 5 combined clinical datasets (Cleveland, Hungary, Switzerland, Statlog, Long Beach VA). 216 medically implausible outliers removed prior to modelling.

Approach: Full logistic regression, Backward Stepwise, and LASSO (cross-validated λ) compared. LASSO selected as primary model — 88.9% sensitivity minimises dangerous false negatives in clinical screening.

Top predictors: ST Slope (Flat/Down), Chest Pain Type (ASY), Exercise-Induced Angina, Oldpeak, and Max Heart Rate — all routinely collected at standard clinical visits, making this a practical screening tool.

Every spring, thousands of students leave behind furniture, electronics, and household goods that end up on curbs — perfectly usable, often barely touched. FurniShift™ is an early-stage concept exploring how to close that loop: connecting people leaving with people arriving, at the right moment, in the right place.

The details are still taking shape. What's clear is the problem — and the window. The rest is being figured out deliberately.
